query: Which method can be used for oxidation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Depositing an atomic layer deposition (ALD) coating with a carefully optimized composition and thickness on a refractory alloy substrate will significantly enhance its oxidation resistance in high-temperature oxidative environments.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy (or similar high-temperature alloy) without any protective surface modification.
generation.intervention: Apply an ultra-thin, uniform ALD coating (e.g., an oxide such as Al2O3 or SiO2) with controlled composition and thickness.
generation.conditions: High-temperature testing under controlled oxidizing atmospheres that simulate service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The ALD coating forms a compact, pinhole-free, protective oxide layer that acts as a diffusion barrier to oxygen.
generation.mechanism: The ALD process provides precise control over the coating’s chemical composition and thickness, enabling the formation of a stable and protective oxide layer that limits oxygen ingress and reduces oxidation of the underlying substrate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Reduced oxidation rate and lower oxide mass gain compared to uncoated samples, with improved retention of mechanical properties after high-temperature exposure.
generation.baseline: Uncoated refractory alloy samples exhibiting typical oxidation kinetics (e.g., higher oxide mass gain and degraded mechanical properties) when exposed to high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness may be limited if the coating is too thin to fully cover the substrate or if significant interfacial stresses develop at extreme temperatures. The precise benefits are dependent on the chosen oxide system and coating thickness.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism is supported by existing studies on surface engineering and ALD, the magnitude of improvement (e.g., percentage reduction in oxidation rate) requires systematic experimental validation across different alloy systems and operating conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical refractory alloy samples: one set with an ALD-deposited oxide coating (optimized for composition and thickness) and one set without any coating. Expose both sets to controlled high-temperature oxidation tests under identical atmospheric conditions for a fixed duration.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and uniformity (via SEM/TEM)
Mechanical property retention (e.g., hardness or compressive strength) after oxidation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ALD-coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (i.e., comparable mass gain, oxide layer morphology, and mechanical property degradation) relative to the uncoated samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Abstract In this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi 2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M 5 Si 3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature. chosen.why: This move directly addresses the open question by implementing a well‐established surface engineering method. ALD enables precise control over the coating parameters (composition and thickness) and allows the study to overcome limitations of earlier studies which may have only partially considered the conditions impacting oxidation resistance. By systematically testing the coatings under realistic high temperature oxidative conditions, the work elucidates the mechanism of protection and validates why such a method can enhance oxidation resistance.
